column4: The source section's dictionary gloss makes olive oil a food given as group provisions; this ayah explicitly joins spending good things earned and produce brought forth from earth, linking cultivated food to its distribution.

The source section names the rain-grown olive in 23:20's food-and-oil scene; this immediately preceding ayah says water is sent down and stored in earth, while 23:19–20 supply the gardens and oil it enables.

The source section calls its fruits and manna forms of rizq; this ayah repeatedly shows Zakariya finding provision with Mary in the sanctuary and her saying it is from God, making unexpected provision concrete.
The source section joins fruit with rain-fed provision; this ayah describes rain-bearing clouds sent to dead land and fruit brought forth from it, a direct growth scene.

The source section recalls fruit asked for in a barren valley; this ayah contrasts good land whose plants emerge by its Lord's permission with poor land yielding little, giving a specific fertile/barren boundary.

The source section's dictionary account describes oil as food provision; Joseph tells the people to sow for seven years and keep most of the harvest in its ears, a specific way of preparing produce as stored sustenance.

The source section describes oil squeezed from olives; after 12:48's famine years consuming the stored harvest, this ayah promises rain and a year when people press produce. The ayah does not identify olives, so the link is the pressing of produce after scarcity.

The source section treats fruit and oil as food provisions; this ayah supplies the stream immediately before 19:25's dates fall and 19:26's instruction to eat and drink, adding water to the meal scene.
The source section treats fruit as edible provision; Mary is told to shake a palm trunk so fresh dates fall to her, a specific scene of fruit given for eating.
The source section joins food with sustenance; after the dates in 19:25, this ayah tells Mary to eat and drink and be comforted, completing the immediate meal scene.
The source section moves from worldly food and provision to unending reward; this ayah joins spending from what God provided with hope for a trade that will never fail.
The source section calls the wage an enduring form of provision; following 35:29's spending and unfailing trade, this ayah says God will repay the workers fully and increase them from His grace.

The source section makes reward the continuing form of provision; this ayah tells the people of the Garden to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did, explicitly making food part of recompense.

The source section joins righteous deeds to an enduring wage; this ayah tells the Garden's people to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they sent ahead, directly connecting nourishment with earned return.

The source section's dictionary entry pictures oil as provisions for a group and its surah grants reward for righteous deeds; this ayah describes the righteous giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for it.

The source section moves from food to reward; after 76:8's feeding of others, this ayah says the givers seek God's face and want neither reward nor thanks from recipients, clarifying the relation between provision and recompense.
The source section moves from fruit as worldly food to an enduring wage; this ayah describes the Garden's shade and fruit made near, a specific food provision within the reward scene.
The source section calls the wage an unending provision; after 76:8–14's giving and Garden scene, this ayah itself identifies the outcome as their reward and their effort as appreciated.
The source section treats fruit as provision and the righteous wage as its lasting counterpart; this ayah names desired fruits among the Garden's gifts that 77:43 then identifies with recompense.
The source section ties righteous deeds to reward; after 77:42's fruit, this ayah tells the people of the Garden to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did.

The source section's oil dictionary branch includes provisions given to a group, and its closing image ties deeds to reward; following the spending passage in 2:262, this ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, setting a boundary on material giving.

The source section labels M-N-N for manna as bestowed food and mamnūn for uninterrupted reward; this ayah uses the root in the distinct sense of reproach after charity and pictures rain stripping soil from a rock, so the gift and the growable yield can both be lost.

The source section explicitly labels Q-W-M as the root behind what sustains a person; this ayah uses the related form qawwāmūn and grounds household responsibility partly in spending wealth, a specific maintenance sense distinct from the section's lexical gloss.

The source section contrasts abundant provision with its loss; following Joseph's storage plan in 12:47, this ayah says the hard years consume the saved harvest, the direct reversal of stored sustenance.

The source section moves from perishable food to an unending reward; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown vegetation that later dries and scatters, immediately before 18:46 names lasting good deeds.

The source section's dictionary gloss pictures oil given as travel provisions; this ayah distinguishes creatures that carry no provision from God's provision for them and for people, sharpening the contrast between carried caravan food and sustenance supplied without being carried.

The source section links a secure sanctuary with fruit brought from every place in 28:57; this ayah says the Haram is made safe while people nearby are seized, giving the boundary of security around that provision scene.

The source section's q-w-m gloss is sustenance that keeps a person standing and suffices; this ayah says provision is sent in measure, since unrestricted abundance would cause transgression, making sufficiency and limit explicit.
The source section treats fruit as edible provision that leads toward enduring reward; this ayah specifies fruits the Garden's people choose, a concrete instance of that provision.

The source section's dictionary entry depicts oil packed as provisions for a traveling group; this ayah joins walking over the earth with eating God's provision, a specific pairing of travel and food.
The source section repeatedly joins a secure sanctuary to fruit and provision; this ayah itself says whoever enters the Sacred House is safe, adding the sanctuary's own safety claim to that meeting.
